blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: The number skills a data question needs: the four operations, scale and representative fractions, mean and range, percentages, ratios and indices, significant figures, scatter relationships, drawing graphs and choosing scales.

blocks.heading: The four operations
blocks.text: Data work is the four operations used as the data requires. Totals by addition: the district's population is its age groups added. Change by subtraction: the growth of the town is this census minus the last. Rates by division: the density is the people divided by the area. Scaling by multiplication: the real distance is the map measurement times the scale. The answer is rounded to suit the figures, because a mean of individual measurements reported to five figures claims a precision the data does not have.

blocks.heading: Scale and representative fractions
blocks.text: A representative fraction such as 1:50 000 means 1 unit on the map is 50 000 of the same units on the ground: 1 centimetre on the map is 50 000 centimetres, which is 500 metres, on the ground. The conversion is multiplication by the denominator and a change to sensible units, and the scale line printed on the map does the same job graphically, which is what the paper edge method uses. On a 1:25 000 sheet, 1 centimetre is 250 metres on the ground.

blocks.heading: Mean and range
blocks.text: The mean is the total of the values divided by how many there are. Five daily rainfalls of 0, 2, 10, 6 and 2 millimetres total 0 + 2 + 10 + 6 + 2 = 20 millimetres, so the mean is 20 / 5 = 4 millimetres. The range is written from the lowest value to the highest, 0 to 10 millimetres, or their difference, 10 - 0 = 10 millimetres, when a single figure is asked for. A range keeps both its ends, its sign and its decimal places: one value alone is not a range, and a minus sign or a decimal dropped loses the precision the question asked to keep.

blocks.heading: Percentages, ratios and decimals
blocks.text: A percentage is the part divided by the whole, multiplied by 100. A town of 40 000 people with 9 000 under 15 has 9 000 / 40 000 x 100 = 22.5 per cent children. A ratio compares parts of a total: 9 000 children and 31 000 others stand in the ratio 9:31. A decimal or fraction converts to a percentage the same way, multiply by 100, so 0.225 is 22.5 per cent. The three forms answer the same question in different clothes, and the data question names which it wants.

blocks.heading: Standard notation and significant figures
blocks.text: Standard notation writes large and small numbers as a figure between 1 and 10 times a power of ten: 8 000 000 000 people is 8 x 10 to the power 9. A negative index marks a fraction: 0.001 is 1 x 10 to the power minus 3. Significant figures count from the first non-zero digit, so 30 400 is 3 to two significant figures but 30 000 to three, and the answer carries the precision the data supports: rainfall gauge readings to the nearest millimetre are not reported to three significant figures as if they were exact.

blocks.heading: Scatter relationships
blocks.text: A scatter graph shows the relationship between two measures, one on each axis. A positive relationship: the points rise together, more of one goes with more of the other, distance from the CBD against house price. A negative relationship: one falls as the other rises, distance from the CBD against land value in most cities. No relationship: the points scatter without a slope, a cloud with no direction. Reading the slope is reading the sign of the relationship, and the points, not the line of best fit alone, are the evidence.

blocks.heading: Drawing graphs
blocks.text: Graphs are drawn to their type. Bars for categories, equal widths, gaps between. Lines for time series, points joined. Divided bars or pie charts for shares of a total. Scatter for relationships. Each point is plotted accurately and each plotted value checked against its scale, because one misread axis scrambles the whole series. The axes are labelled with what they show and the units they show it in.

blocks.heading: Choosing scales and axes
blocks.text: A good graph uses most of the axis length, starts each axis at a value that lets the data fill the grid, and uses simple intervals, 0, 10, 20, 30, that a reader can count in. An axis squashed into the bottom third of the grid wastes the paper and flattens the trend; an axis starting at 0 when the data runs 490 to 510 crams every point into one square. The scale serves the data, and the choice of it is marked as part of the drawing.

blocks.heading: Ruler and protractor
blocks.text: A ruler measures to the nearest millimetre along the line being measured, the zero of the scale set on one end of the line, the reading taken square-on, not at an angle. A protractor's centre sits exactly on the point of the angle, its zero line along one arm, and the reading is taken on the scale that runs clockwise from that zero, the outer scale from the lower arm, the inner from the upper. Bearings use the same discipline: centre on the starting point, zero line along grid north, degrees read clockwise.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: These are the number skills the Paper 4 enquiries of topic 5 need: means and ranges of field data, percentages of survey results, and graphs drawn and scaled for the results tables there.
